content: Pressure ulcers, also known as pressure sores or bedsores, are injuries to the skin and underlying tissues that typically occur over bony areas such as the hips and heels. These injuries result from prolonged pressure and shear forces. Pressure ulcers are associated with significant pain, discomfort, extended hospital stays, and a reduced quality of life. Additionally, they are expensive to treat and place a substantial financial burden on healthcare systems. Importantly, pressure ulcers are largely preventable, and educating patients and their informal caregivers is considered a key strategy in prevention. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of educational interventions directed at patients and/or their informal caregivers on the prevention of pressure ulcers in individuals at risk, across various care settings. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that involved individuals of any age at risk of developing pressure ulcers, as well as RCTs that included informal caregivers of at-risk individuals. The search for relevant studies was conducted in June 2019 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid Embase, Ovid PsycINFO, and EBSCO CINAHL Plus. Clinical trial registries were also searched for ongoing and unpublished studies. No restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or study setting. A total of 10 studies, encompassing 11 publications and involving 2,261 participants, were included in the review. Seven studies focused on interventions targeting individuals at risk of pressure ulcers, measuring outcomes in these individuals. Two studies targeted both at-risk individuals and their family caregivers, measuring outcomes in the at-risk individuals cared for by their families. One study targeted informal caregivers exclusively, measuring outcomes in the at-risk individuals they cared for. The interventions examined in the studies fell into two main categories: the provision of information on pressure ulcer prevention and the implementation of various educational programs. Provision of Information on Pressure Ulcer Prevention: Three studies, involving 237 participants, provided data on this type of intervention. Two studies delivered information directly to at-risk individuals and their caregivers, while the third study provided information to informal caregivers only. Due to the inability to pool data, individual study results were presented. The evidence for the primary outcomes was of very low certainty, downgraded due to study limitations and imprecision. One study compared the use of a self-instruction manual combined with one-on-one patient training and counseling versus a self-instruction manual alone. The results were inconclusive regarding whether this approach reduced the proportion of at-risk individuals developing new pressure ulcers (risk ratio [RR] 0.40, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.14 to 1.18). Another study compared caregiver self-instruction combined with one-on-one counseling versus self-instruction alone. Again, the results were uncertain (RR 2.05, 95% CI 0.19 to 21.70). A third study compared home-based training with routine ward-based training, but it was unclear whether this reduced the proportion of at-risk individuals developing new pressure ulcers (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.27 to 1.02). One study assessed patient knowledge of pressure ulcer prevention as a secondary outcome, but usable data were not provided, preventing further analysis or calculation of an effect estimate. Educational Programs on Pressure Ulcer Prevention: Seven studies, involving 2,024 participants, provided data on educational programs aimed at individuals at risk of pressure ulcers. One secondary report from an included study assessed the primary outcome as the time to pressure ulcer development or occurrence. Three studies and one secondary report assessed the proportion of at-risk individuals developing new pressure ulcers. The evidence suggested no clear difference in the proportion of participants developing new pressure ulcers when comparing a pressure ulcer prevention care bundle (PUPCB) with standard care (hazard ratio [HR] 0.58, 95% CI 0.25 to 1.33). This evidence was of low certainty, downgraded for imprecision. One study explored whether individualized pressure ulcer education combined with monthly structured telephone follow-up affected the mean time to pressure ulcer occurrence. However, not all participants developed pressure ulcers, and the mean time to occurrence could not be calculated. The review found very low certainty evidence regarding the effectiveness of three interventions in reducing the proportion of at-risk individuals developing new pressure ulcers: individualized education with monthly follow-up (RR 0.55, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.30), education delivery (RR 3.57, 95% CI 0.78 to 16.38), and computerized feedback with one-on-one consultations (no clear data provided). Grade of Pressure Ulcer: There was low certainty evidence suggesting that the use of a pressure ulcer prevention care bundle may not significantly affect the severity of new pressure ulcers compared to standard care. Patient Knowledge: The review assessed the impact of various interventions on patient knowledge of pressure ulcer prevention. These included enhanced educational interventions with structured follow-up, motivational interviewing combined with self-management education, the Spinal Cord Injury Navigator program, individualized education with monthly follow-up, computerized feedback, and structured, patient-centered educational events. The evidence for these interventions was of low or very low certainty, with results downgraded due to risk of bias, imprecision, or indirectness. For example, one study reported a mean difference (MD) of 30.15 (95% CI 23.56 to 36.74) in patient knowledge following a structured educational event. Conclusions: The review concluded that there is uncertainty regarding whether educational interventions have any meaningful impact on the development of new pressure ulcers or on patient knowledge. The evidence from the 10 included studies was assessed as being of low or very low certainty due to issues such as risk of bias, serious imprecision, and indirectness. Further research is needed to confirm these findings.
